'''Iva Susan Greenwald''' is an American biologist who is Professor of Cell and Molecular Biology at [[Columbia University]]. She studies cell-cell interactions and cell fate specification in ''[[C. elegans]]''. She is particularly interested in LIN-12/Notch proteins, which are the receptor of one of the major signalling systems that determine the fate of cells.

== Early life and education ==
Greenwald joined MIT as a graduate student in 1977.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last=Greenwald|first=Iva|date=July 2012|title=Notch and the Awesome Power of Genetics|journal=Genetics|volume=191|issue=3|pages=655–669|doi=10.1534/genetics.112.141812|issn=0016-6731|pmc=3389966|pmid=22785620}}</ref> She was trained in the classics of molecular biology and developmental genetics. That year, [[H. Robert Horvitz]] joined the faculty at MIT, and convinced her to investigate ''[[C. elegans]]''. She started working on genetics, and functional redundancy cell-lineage mutants.<ref>{{Cite thesis|title=Genetic studies of muscle structure and cell lineage in Caenorhabditis elegans|date=1982|language=English|first=Iva Susan|last=Greenwald|oclc=10718565}}</ref> She moved to the [[MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology]] in 1983<ref name=":0" /> where she worked alongside [[Jonathan Hodgkin]], [[Gary Ruvkun]] and [[Victor Ambros]], who encouraged her to try to clone LIN-12.<ref name=":0" /> It took her two years to develop a strategy to clone LIN-12 (Tc''1'' transposon tagging), and she identified that that genetic sequence contained [[epidermal growth factor]] (EGF) motifs.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|date=1985-12-01|title=lin-12, a nematode homeotic gene, is homologous to a set of mammalian proteins that includes epidermal growth factor|journal=Cell|language=en|volume=43|issue=3|pages=583–590|doi=10.1016/0092-8674(85)90230-2|issn=0092-8674|doi-access=free|last1=Greenwald|first1=Iva|pmid=3000611}}</ref> These investigations were amongst the first to show that worm developmental genes could be cloned, and that aspects of these genes were homologous to human proteins.<ref name=":1" />

== Research and career ==
In 1986, Greenwald joined the faculty at [[Princeton University]].<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2"/> She moved to [[Columbia University]] in 1993 and became a professor two years later.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|date=2020-09-18|title=Iva S. Greenwald, PhD|url=https://www.cancer.columbia.edu/profile/iva-s-greenwald-phd|access-date=2021-09-04|website=Herbert Irving Comprehensive Cancer Center (HICCC) - New York|language=en}}</ref> Greenwald dedicated her career to understanding the mechanisms that underpin the LIN-12/Notch signalling system.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2"/>  LIN-12/Notch proteins mediate cell-cell interactions. Amongst these processes, Greenwald studies the role of LIN-12/Notich in binary regulation, feedback mechanisms and signal transduction.<ref name=":0" /> She has identified new genes that are involved with the modulation of LIN-12/Notch in development and disease.
